newsitem.title: UK: Studies show how viruses sneak past immune system.
newsitem.headline: Studies show how viruses sneak past immune system.

text.p: Two reports published on Wednesday helped expose some of the disguises used by viruses to sneak past the body's immune system, offering targets to researchers looking for ways to fight them.

Helen Farrell and colleagues at the University of Western Australia said they had found a type of herpes virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), carried a false "flag" that tricks immune system cells into thinking the virus belongs in the body.
Jack Strominger and a team at Harvard University found that in at least one instance the flag was a protein called UL18 that protected it from attack by natural killer cells.
Finding this flag could be an important step to creating drugs that could fight off such viruses. Disabling it could allow the body to destroy viral invaders.
Both teams focused on CMV which can cause blindness and which has become a scourge of AIDS victims.
The virus has a gene that looks just like the gene for major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a large cluster of molecules that helps the immune system recognise foreign invaders.
Farrell's group genetically engineered a virus that infects mice so that the look-alike gene, called m144, was disrupted.
The altered virus could not replicate itself nearly as well as normal viruses and further tests in mice showed natural killer cells were able to destroy the engineered virus.
"Our data indicate that natural killer cells are more effective at restricting replication of (m144) than of wild-type mouse CMV," they wrote.
Strominger's team cited earlier studies that showed human cytomegalovirus could create a surface protein, very close to one made by MHC, which interacted with other molecules such as peptides.

To check and see if UL18 was the key, they first genetically engineered human cells so they had no MHC, leaving them open to attack by the body's immune system because they lacked the "friendly" flag.
Then they spliced in the gene for UL18 and tested whether natural killer cells (NK) would destroy them. They didn't -- so evidently UL18 tricked the natural killer cells.
The researchers said it could be that NK cells had a surface receptor -- a type of keyhole -- that UL18 could plug into and thus fool them into assessing the virus as benign.

Herpes viruses are especially useful for such studies because they are so hard to tackle. Once they infect, they lurk in the body forever, which means they are particularly adept at evading the immune defences.
The family includes herpes varicella, which causes chickenpox and which as herpes zoster causes shingles in adults.
